title: An Education Conservative Is a Liberal Who’s Had To Do Cafeteria Duty? What Nikole Hannah-Jones Misses About Public Education. Plus Fish. ria-duty-what-nikole-hannah-jones-misses-about-public-education-plus
author: Andrew J. Rotherham
summary: Andrew Rotherham gives Nikole Hannah-Jones credit for revisiting her daughter's schooling in public rather than quietly using the carve-outs available to the powerful, and he dismisses much of the criticism as easy dunks. His critique is that the essay is less notable for what it says than for what it omits. She implicates the system but ignores successful public models, popular charter schools, and the teachers contract that makes ineffective teachers hard to remove. She highlights funding inequities while leaving out that her daughter's school spent $52,000 per student with an adult-to-child ratio under ten to one. Rotherham also argues that reducing school quality to race minimizes a problem that traps millions of poor white students too, and that durable reform requires a broad, class-based coalition. He closes by questioning her view that a weak school helped build her daughter's racial identity.
points: Rotherham credits Hannah-Jones for publicly reckoning with a choice she could have quietly reversed.
He faults her lack of curiosity about teacher contracts that protect dangerous and ineffective teachers.
Her school's $52,000 per-pupil spending, he argues, undercuts her emphasis on unequal school finance.
Framing the problem as race alone ignores millions of poor white students in similarly ineffective schools.
He argues academic deficits compound year after year, while pushing back on cultural messages is easier for parents.
quotes: In my view, given her profile, previous writing and past statements, Hannah-Jones deserves credit for doing this in public rather than sweeping it under the rug one way or another.
The article is less compelling for what it says than for what it doesn’t.

Nor does she show much curiosity about the structural causes of the ineffective teaching she so candidly describes. Here’s a hint: it might be a teachers’ contract that makes it hard to fire a dangerous teacher, and harder still to remove one who is merely ineffective at teaching.
This school has an adult to kid ratio of fewer than 10-1 and Hannah-Jones is complaining that the cafeteria was unstaffed and out of control? C’mon.

Perhaps most problematic, she seems not to realize that millions of poor white students are stuck in similarly ineffective schools. Our education quality problem is not simply race-based; it’s also class-based.
In all this, Hannah-Jones may not realize it, but she’s giving cover to the very status quo she claims to decry.
Parents can try, but it’s hard to overcome the compounding deficit of an academically lousy school year after year even with out-of-school services and all the rest.
